## Introduction

This page builds on the [w8b lecture](../week08/w8b_claude.qmd),
where you set up Claude Code in VS Code Server and created a `week08` project dir
with a `CLAUDE.md` file.
Here, you'll learn about additional ways to make working with Claude safer and more effective:
guardrails, memory, skills, and planning.

## Guardrails: Git and permissions {#guardrails}

An agent that can edit files and run commands is powerful, but it can also make mistakes
at a larger scale than a chatbot can.
"Guardrails" are the practices and settings that limit the damage.
Think of the guardrails on a mountain road: they don't stop you from driving,
but they keep you from accidentally going over the edge.

### Git as your safety net

Version control ([week 5](../week05/w5_overview.qmd)) pairs very well with agentic AI:

- **Before** asking Claude for a bigger change, commit your work,
  so that `git status` is clean.
- **After** Claude is done, review _all_ changes with `git diff` or the VS Code
  Source Control panel --- including changes to files you didn't have open.
- **Undo** changes you don't want with `git restore <file>`,
  or discard them in the Source Control panel.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
Claude can write commit messages for you, too
--- but read them, and edit them where needed.
:::

### Built-in protections

By default, Claude Code:

- **Asks before editing files** and before running commands
  (except a set of read-only commands, like `ls`).
- **Asks before accessing files outside your workspace.**
- Tries to detect **"prompt injection"**: instructions hidden in files or web pages that
  Claude reads, which try to make it do something you didn't ask for.
  This protection is not foolproof.

### Permission rules {#permission-rules}

You can add your own rules about what Claude may do, in a `permissions` section of a settings file.
There are three types of rules:

- **allow**: Claude may do this without asking.
- **ask**: Claude must always ask first, even in permission modes that normally don't ask.
- **deny**: Claude may never do this.

For example:

```{.json .file filename=".claude/settings.json"}
{
  "permissions": {
    "ask": [
      "Bash(rm *)",
      "Bash(git push *)"
    ],
    "deny": [
      "Read(~/.claude/settings.json)",
      "Edit(//fs/ess/PAS3493/people/*/garrigos/**)"
    ]
  }
}
```

This example:

- Makes Claude always ask before **removing files** or **pushing to GitHub**.
- Prevents Claude from reading your user settings file, which contains your **API key**.
- Prevents Claude from editing anything in your **raw data** dir.

Where you put these rules determines where they apply:

| File | Applies to |
| ---- | ---------- |
| `~/.claude/settings.json` | All your projects (this is where your API key is) |
| `.claude/settings.json` in a project | That project; commit it to share the rules with collaborators |
| `.claude/settings.local.json` in a project | That project, just for you (don't commit it) |

: {.striped .hover tbl-colwidths="[45, 55]"}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
When you choose "Yes, and don't ask again" for a command,
Claude saves an allow rule in `.claude/settings.local.json`.
To see all rules that are currently active, and which file each comes from,
type `/permissions` in the prompt box.
:::

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise: Add permission rules

1. Create a file `.claude/settings.json` in your `week08` dir from the w8b lecture with the contents shown above.
2. Start a new conversation, and type `/permissions` to check that the rules are active.
3. Ask Claude:

   > Show me the contents of ~/.claude/settings.json

   What happens?
4. Commit `.claude/settings.json`.
:::

::: callout-warning
#### Guardrails complement your own review, they don't replace it
Permission rules can only block what you thought of in advance.
Keep reading Claude's proposed edits and commands,
especially when you work with data that isn't yours to share.
:::

## Memory {#memory}

### How Claude's memory works

In the lecture, you learned that Claude reads your `CLAUDE.md` at the start of every conversation.
In addition, Claude keeps **memory** notes for itself ("auto memory").
As it works with you, it may save notes about:

- Your **preferences** and **corrections** you've given it
  (e.g., "the user prefers lowercase variable names")
- **Project context** that it can't work out from your files
  (e.g., a deadline, or why a decision was made)

It doesn't save something in every conversation, only things it thinks will be useful later.
When it does, you'll see a message like "Saved 1 memory" in the Claude panel.

The memory is stored separately for each project (each Git repository),
in a dir in your Home dir: `~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/`.
That dir contains an index file, `MEMORY.md`, which is loaded into every conversation
in that project, and one file for each memory, which Claude reads when it needs to.

### Memory vs. `CLAUDE.md`

| | `CLAUDE.md` | Memory |
|-|-|-|
| **Who writes it** | You | Claude |
| **Contains** | Instructions and rules | Things Claude learned while working with you |
| **Where** | In your project (can be committed with Git) | In your Home dir (only for you) |

: {.striped .hover tbl-colwidths="[20, 40, 40]"}

Compared to browser-based chatbots, which may remember general things about you,
this is a big advantage: both `CLAUDE.md` and Claude's memory are specific to each project,
so Claude can pick up where you left off in that project.

If you want Claude to remember something, you can tell it directly:

- _"Remember that ..."_ makes Claude save a memory.
- _"Add this to CLAUDE.md: ..."_ adds it to your `CLAUDE.md` instead.
  This is better for things that collaborators (or your future self) should also know,
  since `CLAUDE.md` is part of your project.

### Viewing and editing memory

Type **`/memory`** in the prompt box to see your `CLAUDE.md` files and memory,
and to open them for editing.
Memory files are plain Markdown, so you can edit or delete them as you like ---
and it's worth checking them now and then, since Claude may have saved something
that's wrong or no longer true.

You can also turn auto memory off with the toggle in `/memory`,
or for a single project by adding `"autoMemoryEnabled": false` to the project's
`.claude/settings.json`.

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise: Make Claude remember something

1. In your `week08` project, tell Claude:

   > Remember that when I ask you to explain code, I want a short explanation with an example

2. Type `/memory` and find the note Claude saved.
3. Start a new conversation, and ask Claude to explain a line from one of your scripts.
   Did it follow your preference?
4. If you don't want to keep this memory, delete it (e.g., by asking Claude to forget it).
:::

## Skills {#skills}

### What are skills?

`CLAUDE.md` is meant for information that Claude should _always_ know about your project.
But you may also have multi-step procedures or checklists that you only need for
**specific tasks** --- for example, reviewing a script, or checking the outputs of a workflow.
For those, you can create a **skill**.

A skill is a Markdown file called `SKILL.md`, with instructions for one specific task.
Each skill gets its own dir in `.claude/skills` in your project:

```bash-out-solo
week08
├── .claude
│   └── skills
│       └── review-script
│           └── SKILL.md
├── CLAUDE.md
└── scripts
```

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Skills in `~/.claude/skills` instead are available in all your projects.
:::

### What's in a `SKILL.md` file?

A `SKILL.md` file has two parts:

1. **Front matter** between two `---` lines, like the YAML header of a Quarto document.
   Its most important field is the `description`, which Claude uses to decide when the skill
   is relevant.
2. The **instructions**: what Claude should do, and what it shouldn't do.

For example:

```{.markdown .file filename=".claude/skills/review-script/SKILL.md"}
---
description: Review a shell script for errors and for the conventions used in this project.
---

Review the shell script that the user points to:

1. Read the script and check for errors: syntax, unquoted variables,
   wrong paths, and commands or options that may not exist.
2. Check that it follows the shell script conventions in CLAUDE.md.
3. Report confirmed problems first, and optional improvements separately.
4. Don't edit the script, but ask whether the user wants you to apply the fixes.
```

### Using a skill

You can use a skill in two ways:

- **Explicitly**, by typing `/` followed by the name of its dir, e.g. `/review-script`.
- **Automatically**: when your request matches a skill's description,
  Claude will often use the skill without being told to.

::: callout-tip
#### Skills vs. `CLAUDE.md`

| | `CLAUDE.md` | Skill |
|-|-|-|
| **Use for** | Information Claude should always know | Procedures for specific tasks |
| **Example** | Project dirs, script conventions, rules | Reviewing a script, checking outputs |
| **When loaded** | At the start of every conversation | Only when used |

: {.striped .hover tbl-colwidths="[20, 40, 40]"}

Because a skill's instructions are only loaded when needed,
skills can be longer than `CLAUDE.md` without using tokens in every conversation.
:::

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise: Create and use a skill

1. In your `week08` dir, create the file `.claude/skills/review-script/SKILL.md`,
   with the contents shown above.
2. Start a new conversation, type `/review-script`, and point Claude to `scripts/fastqc.sh`.
   Do you agree with its review?
3. Start another new conversation, open `scripts/count_reads.sh`, and ask:

   > Can you check this script for problems?

   Did Claude use the skill? (You should see this in its response.)
4. Improve the skill based on what you saw, for example by adding a check
   that you think is missing. Then commit it.
:::

## Plan mode, models, and effort levels

### Plan first, then act

For bigger tasks, it's often better to have Claude write a **plan** first, before it changes anything.
In **Plan mode** (select it with the permission mode button in the prompt box),
Claude will look around your project, perhaps ask you some clarifying questions,
and write a plan that opens as a Markdown document.
You can then edit the plan, ask for changes, or approve it so that Claude carries it out.

Plans are also a good way to see how model choice and effort level affect Claude's work,
which is what you'll explore in the exercise below.

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise: Compare a "fast" and a "thorough" plan

You'll ask Claude for the same plan twice: first quickly and cheaply,
and then with the most capable model and more effort.
Use the following prompt both times:

```markdown
Write a plan for aligning the FASTQ files in ../garrigos/fastq to the reference genome
in ../garrigos/ref, and then counting the aligned reads to produce a gene count table.
We will run this at OSC with Apptainer containers.
Which alignment and counting programs would you recommend, and why?
```

**Round 1 --- fast:**

1. Switch to **Haiku** with **Low** effort, and select **Plan mode**.
2. Send the prompt, and read the plan. For example:
   How many steps does it have? Does it name specific programs and versions?
   Does it ask you any clarifying questions, or mention uncertainties?

**Round 2 --- thorough:**

3. Start a **new conversation**, so that the first plan doesn't influence this one.
4. Switch to **Opus** with **High** effort, keeping Plan mode on.
5. Send the same prompt, and read the plan with the same questions in mind.

**Discuss:**

- What differences do you notice between the two plans?
- How would you check whether a plan is reasonable and complete?
- How do the plans compare to what @garrigós2025 did?
- Would the "fast" plan have been good enough?

**Don't** let Claude carry out the plans: decline (or simply stop) when it asks to proceed.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
The thorough round uses many more tokens, so don't repeat it too often with your API key.
:::

## Ideas for using agentic AI

So far, we've used Claude for fairly small tasks.
Here are some ideas for what else it can be useful for in your research:

- **Troubleshooting complex errors.**
  Agents can be surprisingly good at following the trail of an error through a complicated
  set of scripts or a workflow.
- **Things that are beyond your ability, but easy to verify.**
  For example, a complicated software installation,
  or automating a tedious, repetitive task.
- **Proofreading code that works.**
  In a large set of scripts, it's easy to miss inconsistent variable names or similar
  small errors --- agents can be quite meticulous at catching these.
- **Writing workflows**, including in formal workflow languages like Nextflow
  (see [week 11](../week11/w11_overview.qmd)).
- **The "optional next steps" you never get to**, such as:
  - Organizing a project dir, writing documentation, and putting it under version control
    (see [week 10](../week10/w10_overview.qmd))
  - Turning a script into a Quarto document (see [week 14](../week14/w14_overview.qmd))
  - Building a personal or lab website with Quarto
- **Keeping a log.** For longer projects, ask Claude to keep a log file
  (e.g., `LOG.md`) of what it did and why, which helps both you and future
  conversations with Claude.

Looking for ideas beyond coding?
[This site by a political scientist](https://claudeblattman.com) is one starting point.

## Other ways to use Claude Code

- **In the terminal**: Claude Code is also a command-line program (`claude`),
  which has the same features and uses the same settings files.
- **In other editors**: The extension also works in editors based on VS Code,
  such as Positron, an editor for R and Python.
